newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine business to meet unions on labor reform.
newsitem.headline: Argentine business to meet unions on labor reform.

text.p: Argentina's Group of Eight business lobby, in a meeting with government officials on Tuesday, agreed to begin talks with trade unions aimed at reaching consensus on proposed labor reforms.

Jorge Blanco Villegas, head of the Argentine Industrial Union (UIA), told reporters that the heads of the main business and industry chambers accepted the government request for three-way talks with the main CGT labor federation.

Business leaders meeting with Cabinet Chief Jorge Rodriguez, Interior Minister Carlos Corach and Labor Minister Armando Caro Figueroa also agreed to discuss the use of black market labor and tax evasion with labor leaders.
Rodriguez, confirming the three-way talks, emerged from the meeting insisting the 17.3 percent unemployment rate was of "particular concern" to the government.
No date was set for meetings but they were expected to begin next week.
The Peronist government and the main CGT labor federation, at loggerheads over plans to fight unemployment by changing labor law, agreed last week to resume dialogue.

After the CGT on December 26 led its third general strike of last year, President Carlos Menem signed three decrees reducing union control of collective pay bargaining. Other reforms, such as replacing redundancy payouts with unemployment insurance, are more palatable to the unions and were to be thrashed out in Congress.
But Argentine labor courts threw out the decrees, calling them unconstitutional, and Menem's ministers ask the CGT to come back to the negotiating table.
Menem, who faces tough mid-term elections in Congress in October, argues that only the "flexibilization" of labor laws can help create jobs.
But the unions fear he means to reduce their power and take away worker rights.

After Menem on the weekend irked employers by saying they were "not being active enough in creating jobs," CGT chief Rodolfo Daer says he would take a whole "list of demands" on employment policy into the three-way talks. ((-- Gary Regenstreif, Buenos Aires newsroom, 541 318-0618))
